card.title: Running a chemical plant; designing a chemical plant

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A chemical plant is a network of unit operations arranged around a few unit processes, sized by mass and energy balances that make it verifiable on paper and diagnosable in operation. Design runs flowsheet → balances → equipment → materials → safety → siting, with inherent safety placed before engineered protection and alarms — ordered by reliability, not gadgetry.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Mass balance: Σ inputs = Σ outputs + accumulation (= 0 at steady state) - Energy balance: Σ heat in = Σ heat out + duty removed/added

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Covers only: running a chemical plant, designing a chemical plant (within Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: A plant at steady state is a mass and energy balance being satisfied every second.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The separations share*** - the reactor is a few cubic metres; the distillation train, exchangers and filters occupy the rest - most of the plant is physical, not chemical.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Designing and Running a Chemical Plant A chemical plant is a **network of unit operations** — reactors, absorbers, distillation columns, heat exchangers, filters, pumps — arranged by a process flowsheet. Designing one means choosing the operations, sizing them by mass and energy balances, selecting materials, and engineering safety in; running one means keeping that network at its designed…  ·  ## 2. Theorem Mirror - **Design sequence:** (1) process flowsheet — the reaction route drawn as connected unit operations; (2) mass balance — atoms in = atoms out for every unit; (3) energy balance — heat duties for every exchanger, reactor, column; (4) equipment selection and sizing; (5) materials of construction (corrosion, temperature, pressure); (6) safety engineering (relief, containment, control interlocks);…

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: The mass balance makes the plant verifiable on paper - and makes operational losses diagnosable in operation.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Design sequence: flowsheet -> mass balance -> energy balance -> equipment sizing -> materials -> safety -> layout/siting. Unit operations (physical: distillation, filtration, absorption, drying) vs unit processes (chemical: nitration, hydrogenation). Most plant volume and cost is separations, not reaction.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Inherent safety outranks protective equipment: the safest plant is the one with the least hazard to protect against.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Deep Conceptual — The Plant as a Balanced Network, Not a Machine - The flowsheet's discipline is the **balance**: every unit operation obeys "in = out" for mass and energy, and the design arithmetic is these balances applied unit by unit.…  ·  ## 4. Deep Conceptual — Safety Is Designed In, Not Bolted On - The design sequence places safety after materials but *before layout* deliberately: relief valves, containment, interlocks, and inherently safer choices (less hazardous solvent, milder conditions, smaller inventory) are cheapest at the flowsheet stage and impossible to retrofit cheaply.…  ·  ## 5. Worked Example Types - **Type A — flowsheet reading:** identify unit operations and unit processes in a given scheme. - **Type B — mass balance arithmetic:** simple in–out with recycle. - **Type C — siting argument:** justify a plant location against the factor list. - **Type D — safety hierarchy:** order protective measures by the inherent-safety principle.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: List the siting factors for a new fertiliser plant and rank the top three.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **"Unit operation and unit process are synonyms":** operations are physical, processes are chemical — distillation vs nitration. **"Safety means alarms":** alarms are the last layer; inherent safety (less hazardous inventory) is the first.
